newsitem.title: BANGLADESH: Bangladesh shares fall amid manipulation charges.
newsitem.headline: Bangladesh shares fall amid manipulation charges.

text.p: Thousands of distraught share traders, saying they were victims of market manipulators, protested outside Bangladesh's Dhaka Stock Exchange (DSE) on Tuesday as slumping stock prices threatened to ruin them.

Police guarded the bourse during the demonstration by the traders, most of whom operate in the unofficial kerb market, amid rumours that an impending official report would implicate big market players in share price manipulation.

Officials with the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) said the report on the alleged manipulation -- said to have been responsible for the market soaring to record levels last year -- would be submitted on Thursday.
The government appointed a committee in December to investigate the unusual rise in share prices during October and November and the market's subsequent nosedive.
One protester, Delwar Hossain, charged that the delay in submitting the report was giving manipulators time to pack up their businesses and escape the falling market.
"Most unemployed and educated youths came to the capital market with their small savings or borrowed money. Now they are paupered," he told Reuters.
Stock trader Mohammad Arefin said manipulators were taking advantage of the delay in announcing the report.
M. Bodiuzzaman, another investor, said he lost two thirds of the 1.5 million taka (US$35,000) he had invested in shares.
"I was employed in a Middle East country and returned home with the money hoping to make a fortune."
Traders in the kerb market demanded the immediate release of the inquiry report and the setting up of a national stock exchange to restore investor confidence.
Abul Khair said his capital dwindled to 400,000 taka from the 1.7 million taka he invested after returning from a job in Germany. "I cannot even find buyers for the shares."
The DSE all-share price index closed down 86.52 points, or 6.97 percent, at 1,153.52 on a turnover of 70.6 million taka on Monday.

The market began its heady ascent soon after general elections last June that brought Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina to power. Between June and November, the DSE benckmark index jumped from less than 1,000 to more than 3,600.
Market analysts blame the government for failing to take action when share prices were unreasonably high without any basis such as the economic fundamentals of listed companies.
Broker Shakil Rizvi said the government could have offloaded its shares in dozens of public companies to calm the overheated market and check the spiralling prices.
